So, just finished this one and must say I'm quite satisfied with the whole experience, although it could be a bit bigger and perhaps juuust a bit more cmplicated when it comes to the story itself, but I guess this is a start - a game like this deserves a regular Agatha Christie as a story-writer, hope they find one. Regarding the game mechanics themself, game is really user-friendly and becomes a bit frustrating only at the end itself when you're trying to think about the best way to finish all this and all the options seem wrong, but I can't say if I'm glad or mad that this was made in this way. Anyway, Orwell is a great piece of software, not only for the gaming experience but I truly believe that there is a potential of using this product as a didactical tool for getting into kids minds what the posibilities of an online person tracking are - Orwell is a great lecture on "internet privacy" - ok, maybe a step or two high on paranoid dreams, but not so far away from the truth. The creation of the internet is the most technological advance tool mankind has ever made, right next to toilets. With the modern age of technology we have today, the effects on our lives stack up as the age-old question Security vs. Freedom comes into the debate again.  I am talking about a game where it tackles the subject on privacy issues which is Orwell. There will be a spoiler section on the comments to give my personal thoughts on some episodes. I will give an analytical review of this game and give in my two cents if this plays well as it was intended. 

[h1]CHECKING YOUR ID[/h1]

You play as Snowden-I MEAN the investigator, you work for the government and try a new technology called Orwell. You checked on people’s devices and try to add data chunks that matter on a case you are specifically working on. To be frank, in the first episode I was intrigued by the concept of the machine, it felt the game was really inspired by the true story of Edward Snowden about the CIA scandal. Now, the difference from the actual real event and the game is that the game focus on only the investigator and your co-worker trying to solve this case together. You the investigator only see the dirty secrets while your advisor Symes only advice you on your next tasks or comment on your search. I will explain a bit more detail but it will have to be in the spoiler section on why Orwell works like that.

[h1]BACKGROUND CHARACTERS AND STORY[/h1]

I have to cut a lot to avoid spoilers so I will give you a summary of the story but will give you how the characters and their world behave. The story is interesting for how it was trying to show the concept of privacy. I absolutely love how each character from the profiles you investigate shows a unique dialogue from each text you read from different characters. They feel almost exactly like how people should talk especially on the internet. When you read each email, phone calls etc. you can picture actual people having a real conversation which is great! It never made you feel like the dialogue felt artificial or fake, like adults “trying” to sound what people would say on the internet. I also love how they try to implement how people would sound like on the comment sections and insert memes along the way. 

The art style is another unique aspect of the game of how it shows a polygonal art style look. Most of the faces are fine though some were not as quite good in certain looks like some faces of the characters you profile are a bit strange with their beady eyes or mouth. The music is quite good giving you a sense of futuristic vibe to it while also gives you a dread feeling where certain events happen during your case. You even have one shot whatever you send data chunks to Symes and you can’t go back to it even exit the game won’t do. Whatever you send to Symes will affect the characters that you are working on the case. Which now I will talk about the actual meat of the review, the concept of the game and the driving point of Orwell.

[h1] THE CHOICE IS YOURS[/h1]

The focus of what the developers are getting at is the whole anti-surveillance vs. freedom. The story hints you that the Nation (that is the country of this game) is trying to add more cameras after the safety bill was passed and some foreign problem that led to mass immigration, based on what the articles within the game said. The game even tried to give you signs that you are “supposedly” working for the bad guy and that the group that you were assigned to follow name [i]Thought[/i] is the good guys because they believe in Freedom of Speech and you are trying to incriminate them. How exactly you are incriminating them is because of how Orwell is set up to be. Orwell is a super-computer that analyze information and even interpret the information for you to post it. Unfortunately, because of how Orwell acts according to its programming it will translate the language the program will find it logical. Which leads to falsify the context that was given if you don’t read their messages clearly because remember, only you know the truth and Symes is only there as your advisor so he won’t know the full context of your side of the truth, only Orwell.  That is why it can be easy for people to get arrested just because Symes read what you send base on Orwell translated. Is this good?

 Well at first I almost had a problem with It because why the developers put it that way, but later as I finished the game I realized this was purposefully done this way and it was the right call. The purpose of their message is that people have way too much confidence of a machine to do their jobs for you they forgot how machines can be the dumbest tools for interpreting human language which they probably will never understand unless you are human. This is why in real life there are moderators to keep track of reports of people saying certain stuff. Bots can detect it but when humans actually read the context of their side of the story the problem is fix. The game did a great job of showing how humans rely on Orwell too much, but what I’m most impress is why they design the game to make it only you see the whole truth. 

In my playthrough I played the game like it was real life, I pretend I actually worked for the government and I role-play as an investigator, although sometimes I break my role to send certain data chunks that have nothing to do with the case but to pull Symes hair on certain funny comments. Anyway, when you sit down and do your “job” to be the eye on everyone’s business, not to joke around I felt pressure on taking the responsibility on sending people’s privacy, even if it means breaking some moral codes for the good of saving lives. I somehow felt like a god knowing people’s secrets and manipulate their lives on sending whatever data it comes and I send that data to Symes so that he take action to do something of this person. I can see why having this kind of power is utter madness to have, but at the same time is it really crazy to have this power?

 The game gives you a clear sense of black and white of giving you choices to follow, either be pro-government by pleasing them everything you send or follow your own thoughts of which is good and bad. Certainly, nobody here is good at least for the group [i]Thought[/i], I wish Symes would talk more of his stance of the government trying to make people safe like he would talk about how certain parts of giving up freedom for security is good even if they don’t understand. This would create an even more dilemma which the game has but certain parts fail which leads to my last discussion. 

How it handles the 1984 concepts. I felt they only scratch the surface of what it truly means for giving up your freedom. [i]Thought[/i] members tell you how bad cameras but they don’t know how the cameras are being used, they just say is bad because of privacy reasons. One member says they love the freedom of speech but at the same time I don’t see the government censoring their citizenships, maybe their newspaper but nothing more am I missing something? I heard they have immigration problem so why not show more articles showing the effects of the safety bill. Are they discriminate more by taking away their privacy than the Nation’s citizens?

 Do the immigrants have the same freedom as the Nation?  These are questions they sort of tell but just not the amount where the players really ask themselves if freedom does have a cost or that if security has its perk for saving citizens, where is the line on that. To me, it felt like a basic philosophy lesson about Orwellian which does not go as deep as I thought.  

In the end is still a great game to start with the season, the concept is interesting and even the certain parts of the game felt too real of how our world functions in terms of responding of cameras everywhere. This game deserves a 7/10! Recommend for a good short time experience for a fan of dystopian settings.

What an incredible game. I sat down hoping to start and finish a game in one sitting, and I did just that, just over 6 and a half hours later.

The game has you scouring websites and messages to begin with, later involving phone calls and electronic devices too. This action tickles a very specific investigative soft spot, allowing you to accept or reject information as you see fit (with some plot-progression-required points aside). Unfortunately this comes with the caviat that your -intention- is not always understood when making these choices, but the game does the best it can to inform you how the data will be interprited, while staying in-universe.

Now I have to make this very clear: I thought this game was completely different, based on the trailer I watched. I thought I would be monitoring areas using CCTV and pulling up profiles on potential criminals with Watchdogs-style hackery. This couldn't be further from the truth - this is an interactive visual novel through-and-though, much like a previous game I've played, and would highly recommend, Analogue: A Hate Story.

While playing this game I felt genuine emotions, which does not happen often. I felt elation at preventing an attack--something I felt I had complete control over, not just interaction with--and guilt over a death--one I know I caused, but could have potentially stopped with information I realised I had overlooked too late. It's like a more relaxed version of Telltale's The Walking Dead games, where your choices have sincere impact on the world. But don't think it's all just casual browsing either, as there are timed occurances that you need to be quick on your mouse to prevent, should you choose to. Sometimes you have to make uninformed choices, which you will simply have to live with the consequences of, while giving you hindsight for future playthroughs.

All in all, it was a fascinating story and premise that kept my attention for its duration, with the clear possibility of replayability, should you want to see all possible outcomes (and right your wrongs). You couldn't ask for more than that.

Orwell is an overall good game that tells an interesting story.  I thoroughly enjoyed it, being a simple narrative journey with very little direct gameplay.  You play as an investigator for the government of The Nation, charged with monitoring the Orwell survellience system.  It's your job to investigate an attack on the Nation, and feed what you think is pertinent information to your advisor.  Will you bring the criminals to justice, or help them get away?  Your choices matter in this one, and I can honestly say that the choices are significant enough to change how things shake out as the story progresses.  I highly recommend trying out the demo episode and, if you enjoy it, picking this one up even at full price.

Pros:
- Broken out into 5 episodes, so it can be enjoyed in chunks easily, or binged all at once
- Simple gameplay mechanics.  Its a slight variation on your average point and click
- Interesting narrative with choices that actually have an impact on the outcomes in the end.  The information you choose to pass will make a difference!
- Unique art style

Cons:
- If point and click isn't your thing, this isn't for you
- I had some issues with clicking on information, as it was sometimes unresponsive and would not allow me to drag the info into the necessary area
- Repeat playtroughs get a little frustrating when you are forced to sit through the "animations" of the phone calls and texts

Overall a solid, entertaining game.

For instance, I missed that one character had a boyfriend and thus I also missed that the boyfriend died. This wasn't required to finish the game, but it's a tidbit I unlocked by making different choices!
I LOVE THIS GAME AND I HOPE THE SEQUEL IS JUST AS FUN!
My ONLY NEGATIVE FEEDBACK is that YOU CANNOT SKIP THE LONG CHATS-specifically the 9 1/2 minute group chat at the end. So, if you're after those achievements MAKE SURE YOU HAVE SOMETHING TO DO while the game runs through nearly ten minutes of chatting that you can't quicken or skip. The only change to the dialogue is if you free Cassie and her boo Josef. Otherwise, it's the exact same pony show for TEN. MINUTES. But that's my ONLY GRIPE with the game!

VERY intertaining! LOVELY art, and EASY TO USE interface! And, when you're a newb, the tutorial is almost not even needed. VERY EASY to pick up how this game works! 15/10!!!!!!
Great game. Not the longest, but its fun, engaging, and has replayability. So anyone who likes choices matter games, you should get this :)

The story was interesting, for a while, but the pacing drove me crazy. The slow slow scrolling of text that you can't speed up or fast load just killed the game for me. If you read faster than a 6th grader you're going to spend most of your 'gameplay' waiting on text.

Also, gameplay is very liberal. This is a story with minor interaction. Again, interesting, but not good in terms of gaming.

Story: 3/10. No, sorry. I don't buy it. The characters weren't believable, and frankly I didn't care about any of them.

Fun: 3/10. Zzzzzz. 
 
Penalties: 0/10. Nothing to comment.

The issue here is that you don't really detect or solve anything. You just click on all the clues and then move on to the next chapter. It's like an interactive story, and frankly the story isn't that great. There might have been some great idea in this concept, but the final product is just dull as dishwater.

_Orwellian 'Her Story'_

Very short, but an intriguing cast of characters and linear yet entertaining decisions.

Only negative is the very short play time of around 2 hours.

Still recommded for everyone, especially more casual players in it for a good interactive story.

this is a puzzle game, very short(2.5 hours), and with poor replayability. do not buy unless there is a large discount and you liked the demo. 

the problem is that you have very limited control of the story, and this focuses much more on what you choose not to upload. at several points, you do not move forward until specific options are uploaded. a lot of the choices have consequences in later days that are not initially obvious, and there are many red herrings. there are multiple endings, and thus you need to replay if you want the acheivements. 

the story is well written, but relies on hidden information that is revealed in the last chapter, and on plot twists. none of that works well past the first playthrough.
It has no gameplay whatsoever.  I don't recommand this junk, it's not a game.  It more like a timeline of a story.  It's linear and has no options.

So where aspects of this game are a little cheezy, the structure of the UI and gameplay is excellent.  The storyline is a bit on the linear side, but thankfully you only see this in retrospect as you play through the game and you see how you've been manipulated into an outcome.  For the price I paid for this (on Steam Sale), it is brilliant and I've gotten more than my money's worth.  This franchise deserves a lot more attention than it's getting.
A great interactive story, the gameplay mechanic suits your role perfectly. Played this game twice, once as a proper force of justice and the second and as a distrustful dystopian snoop.

Wonderful story, especially in an age where 24/7 government surveillance isn't unthinkable (in terms of technology). If you enjoy sifting through data, painting a specific picture using the information you find, and a very text-heavy, story-driven experience with branching narratives, then this is the game for you. It's also quite possible to mess around with it, and there are plenty of achievements for playing the game differently perhaps than originally intended. Well worth the low price, and then some!
One of the best game i have played.

Would you pay $4 to sit through a an average dystopian movie that covers no new ground? do you like point and click games? then you'll like this! This game is short and has little replay value. I would absolutely not recommend it at its full price, but on sale it's a matter of taste. The art/design of the video game was good, in that it did what it wanted to accomplish well. The writing style was fitting and well done, but the story itself was lackluster and unsatisfying. 

I'm giving it a 6/10. it runs well, looks good, and accomplished what it wanted to accomplish.

Got this game + ignorance is strength on sale for $8.98. Totally worth it. More like an interactive thriller than a game though. Didn't feel I had many options to really screw things up. I pretty much finished it in 5 hours (straight). Going to try the expansion tomorrow, although I've read it's not as good as the original. I am satisfied with Orwell, again, taking in cosideration I paid under $10 for it. Also I just read there's multiple endings (?), so... I'll play it again, definitely.

I just played the game again, with a completly different outcome. Buy this game now that it's cheap, it's great!

Personally, I loved this game. It's a quick experience and there isn't really any replayability, but it was hard to put down once it picked up the pace. It's not highly interactive, making it a touch of a drag-and-click style walking simulator, but the story and the characters were very interesting. When it finally raised the stakes a little, it genuinely inspired feelings of urgency. Like I said, however, one downside it has is that it's really hard to play it again. The tutorial is well integrated into the story of the game, but on another playthrough it feels incredibly tedious and like you just want to get going. There are a lot of ways the game can go differently, and while intreging to pursue some of the alternate routes, it's hard to want to slough through a lot of the same dialogue I saw before.

Great game! Great story-telling! You really feel like you're a part of this world. The choices you make heavily impact the story. It does require a decent amount of concentration and a lot of reading, so you should probably take a few breaks to avoid eye-strain.
This game is a good general idea, could use some work and its very short, Beat it in a day but i still liked it.

A game about ideas that manages to tie gameplay to its ideas. While the gameplay is pretty light, I enjoyed the story the game told and found the simple but compeling puzzle aspects interesting. I wish the game did a little more to make your choices feel more impactful throughout as I felt like simply sending everydata chunk to advance my collection of options other than the yellow data chunks. While some may find the game unenjoyable if they aren't okay with being a light participant in a terrorist plot and require deep gameplay, the story was interesting enough to keep me personally hooked.

I also enjoyed the themes of the game and how the gameplay reflected that. You can choose to do diferent things that will affect how events turn out and because of those choic es the game reveals ideas about cyber security and privacy. Surveillance culture and how you feel about it can show through the game and I really like that in games. I don't think this game is for everyone but if the themes seem interesting at all to you then you'll probably find this game interesting.

a friend gifted me this as it had been sitting on my wishlist a while.  needless to say i wish i'd played it sooner because it was better than i expected and it was a nice short game which while some might not prefer i find refreshing. it seemed like there were a good few choices i could have made vs what i did choose so theres probably a replayability factor thats good to it but i don't tend to replay many things so if i do it'll have to wait.  this said i'm intrested in the next 'season' of it at some point to be sure.
I spent $5 to cure my boredom.  This game did the opposite.
Well, it's something different for a change. Get it if you really want to find out for yourself.
A tense and gripping story which helps us questions the ethics of modern surveillance. Soundtrack is also great

Wow, some games really leave an impact and this is one of them!  One of the most truely immersive games I've played in a long time. Proof that games can be art as much as any book or film, and there are some things that the medium can explore in ways non-interactive media can only dream of.
Recommended for fans of 'detective' games, people who don't mind reading, and anyone who wants to feel like their choices really really matter.  
Also for anyone with even a passing interest in electronic surveilance, which should really be all of us!

Awesome!
This game is a brilliantly woven tapestry, its clever and subtle. Its engaging, thrilling and revealing. The game appears linear, but you will gradually realize how you control the narrative as you play. This game swallows you up in a sophisticated mystery. The theming reminded me of Papers, Please, but not the gameplay. I reached the end of the game, and I already want to play it all over again. I will definitely buy the next episode and probably every episode after. This game deserved to win awards, and if anything it is still underappreciated!

I would say this game has a broad appeal, and many people would like this who would not be able to tell that they would from the beginning. I suspect this game is a bit unique, there really isnt anything like this. 
Strong recommendation to everyone! Download the demo, and you'll see.
